Match-E-Be-Nash-She-Wish Band of Potawatomi Indians

The Match-E-Be-Nash-She-Wish Band, commonly called the Gun Lake Tribe, has its own Potawatomi community history. The Tribe’s heritage account follows movement from the Kalamazoo Valley toward the Bradley settlement and describes continuity through pressures for removal and later recognition efforts. A conservation-agency account adds a narrowly scoped reading route into present relationships with rivers and lake sturgeon. These perspectives introduce this named Band without treating all Potawatomi communities as a single government.

01

Kalamazoo Valley and Bradley

The heritage narrative links the Band’s history to the Kalamazoo Valley and a settlement near Gun Lake. Its treaty and recognition summaries should lead readers toward the underlying records, rather than serve as a current-rights or boundary determination.

Read the sources [1] Gun Lake Tribe / Match-E-Be-Nash-She-Wish Band of Pottawatomi

02

Continuing work with waterways

The Fish and Wildlife Service names Gun Lake and Little River among its Michigan lake-sturgeon partners. This records a particular collaboration; it does not establish present population recovery, universal cultural practice or the outcome of every project.

Read the sources [2] U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service; Zachary Locklear

Heritage — Gun Lake Tribe History ↗

The Tribe recounts its Kalamazoo Valley and Bradley-settlement history and recognition process. Its narrative is a starting community perspective; treaty implementation and legal characterizations need separate comparison.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Complete visible history narrative19–32 and historic timeline33–140 read. Synthesis uses Kalamazoo/Bradley continuity and institutional history, not current officeholders, programme outcomes, contested legal descriptions or a full treaty review.

Working with Tribal Partners to Achieve Shared Conservation Goals ↗

An agency account of named Tribal partnerships, including Little River and Gun Lake sturgeon work. It supplies a conservation perspective rather than an entire community history.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Complete visible article body, lines170–190, read; synthesis uses the named Michigan partnerships at188–189. Linked projects, monitoring datasets and reported outcomes were not independently audited. No current population, legal-rights or programme-success determination.
